name: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System

clinicalPearls: The autonomic nervous system has parasympathetic (craniosacral), sympathetic (thoracolumbar, T1-L2), and enteric divisions; acetylcholine is the preganglionic transmitter for both arms and the postganglionic parasympathetic transmitter, while norepinephrine is the postganglionic sympathetic transmitter (except eccrine sweat glands, which use acetylcholine).

Dysautonomia is best classified clinically by organ specificity (heart, vessels, sweat glands, pupils, gastrointestinal, genitourinary) and by time course (acute/subacute/chronic, progressive/static), which helps narrow the differential.

Classical orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall of systolic BP >=20 mmHg or diastolic BP >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt >=60 degrees; in hypertensive patients the threshold is >=30/15 mmHg.

Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is suggested by a blunted compensatory heart-rate rise (<15 beats/min); a heart-rate-rise/systolic-BP-fall ratio below 0.5 beats/min/mmHg after 3 minutes more accurately indicates neurogenic OH and reflects impaired cardiac baroreflex gain.

POTS is defined as chronic (>3 months) orthostatic intolerance WITHOUT sustained orthostatic hypotension, with a heart-rate rise of >=30 beats/min (>=40 if under age 19) or a rate above 120 beats/min within 10 minutes of standing; it is a sinus-rhythm disorder, four to five times more common in women aged 15-45.

About half of POTS cases follow a viral illness (notably EBV, coronavirus, enteroviruses); it is the leading manifestation of long COVID, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome predisposes in up to 25% of patients.

Heart-rate variation to deep breathing tests the vagal (parasympathetic) baroreflex arm; the Valsalva maneuver assesses both parasympathetic (Valsalva ratio) and sympathetic (adrenergic index, BP recovery) arms; both are diminished in most autonomic failure, diabetes, and alpha-synuclein disorders.
Sudomotor localization: a postganglionic lesion shows absent sweating on BOTH QSART and thermoregulatory sweat test (TST), whereas a preganglionic lesion preserves QSART but shows anhidrosis on TST.

Multiple system atrophy (Shy-Drager) combines autonomic failure with parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar features (MSA-C); the parkinsonism responds poorly/transiently to levodopa and rest tremor is not prominent.

Cardiac sympathetic innervation imaging (MIBG scintigraphy or fluorodopamine PET) is typically PRESERVED in MSA but reduced in Parkinson disease, Lewy body disease, and pure autonomic failure, aiding differentiation.

Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy is a treatable cause associated with high-titer antibodies to the alpha-3 ganglionic acetylcholine nicotinic receptor; it may be paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer, thymoma, lymphoma), so malignancy screening is prudent.
Autonomic dysreflexia is a dramatic BP surge triggered by bladder, bowel, or skin irritation in spinal cord lesions above T6; lesions below T6 permit splanchnic vasodilation and rarely cause it.
harrison.pathophysiology: The autonomic nervous system operates as an integrated reflex circuit linking sensory feedback from organs with central processing (insular and prefrontal cortex, limbic system, hypothalamus; brainstem nucleus tractus solitarius, dorsal motor vagal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus) and the spinal intermediolateral cell columns, then to peripheral ganglia and target organs. Dysfunction may arise from decreased activity, overactivity, or dysregulation at the afferent limb, central processor, or efferent limb. In orthostatic hypotension, standing shifts roughly 500-700 mL of blood to the lower limbs and splanchnic bed; the normal compensatory baroreflex (slight tachycardia, veno- and arteriolar constriction) maintains pressure, and neurogenic OH results from inadequate peripheral norepinephrine release with loss of vascular tone. The synucleinopathies (MSA, Parkinson disease with autonomic failure, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure) share aggregation of misfolded, phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in central and peripheral autonomic structures; MSA characteristically shows glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes (versus neuronal Lewy bodies in PD/LBD), with possible prion-like cell-to-cell transfer. Peripheral autonomic neuropathies damage small myelinated and unmyelinated sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. POTS pathophysiology is heterogeneous, including distal sympathetic denervation with preserved cardiac sympathetic function (neuropathic POTS), venous pooling, hypovolemia, deconditioning, altered baroreflex regulation, and sympathetic overactivity.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple system atrophy (MSA-P and MSA-C / Shy-Drager syndrome)
Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies with autonomic failure
Amyloid autonomic neuropathy (AL and hereditary transthyretin)
Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy and seronegative autoimmune autonomic neuropathy
Familial dysautonomia (Riley-Day) and hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies
Spinal cord lesions (trauma, syringomyelia, subacute combined degeneration, MS/NMO) with autonomic dysreflexia
Baroreflex failure (e.g., after neck irradiation injuring carotid sinus baroreceptors)
Fabry disease and POTS related to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
infectionMimics: Post-viral POTS following EBV, coronavirus, or enteroviral illness (and long COVID)
Botulism producing cholinergic failure (blurred vision, sluggish pupils, dry mouth, ileus, urinary retention)
nonInfectiousMimics: Medication and supplement effects (diuretics, antihypertensives, tricyclics, antipsychotics, dopamine agonists; sympathomimetic supplements causing tachycardia/hypertension)
Pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism mimicking POTS sympathetic activation
Primary cardiac arrhythmias and chronotropic insufficiency
Sjogren sicca syndrome resembling muscarinic failure
Low-pressure CSF headache versus orthostatic headache of OH
additionalInvestigations: Orthostatic vital signs (supine and standing BP/HR at 1 and 3 minutes); tilt-table testing for orthostatic intolerance and syncope subtyping
Heart-rate variation to deep breathing and Valsalva maneuver for cardiovagal and adrenergic baroreflex function
QSART and thermoregulatory sweat test to localize sudomotor (pre- vs postganglionic) lesions
Skin punch biopsy (2-4 mm) for epidermal nerve fiber density and intraneural alpha-synuclein deposition
Supine and upright plasma catecholamines (failure to rise on standing in central/preganglionic; low supine and no rise in postganglionic)
Nutritional/metabolic labs: B12, folate, vitamin D, iron/ferritin, and in GI involvement thiamine, B6, niacin, riboflavin, vitamin C, vitamin E, copper, coenzyme Q10, carnitine
2-hour glucose tolerance test in small-fiber neuropathy with normal HbA1c (impaired glucose tolerance is a frequent cause)

Serum free light chains and protein electrophoresis for amyloidosis; autoantibodies (ganglionic AChR alpha-3, voltage-gated K and P/Q Ca channel, plexin, GAD); paraneoplastic panel (anti-Hu, CRMP5, amphiphysin)
Brain MRI in suspected MSA (striatal iron in MSA-P; cerebellar/pontine atrophy with 'hot cross bun' sign in MSA-C); MIBG scintigraphy or fluorodopamine PET to distinguish MSA from PD/LBD/PAF
5-HIAA for carcinoid; rheumatologic screen (Sjogren, scleroderma, mixed connective tissue disease); genetic testing for porphyria, Fabry, TTR mutations
redFlags: Impaired olfaction, impaired balance, abnormal movements, and dream-enactment sleep behavior (apnea, stridor) signal a degenerative extrapyramidal/synucleinopathy disorder
Symptomatic orthostatic hypotension within 2 years of parkinsonism onset, early urinary and erectile dysfunction, and rapid disability progression favor MSA over idiopathic Parkinson disease
Supine hypertension with reverse dipping in autonomic failure predicts end-organ (renal, cardiac, cerebrovascular) damage
Autonomic dysreflexia BP surges above a T6 cord lesion can precipitate intracranial vasospasm or hemorrhage
Life-threatening cardiovascular dysautonomia in Guillain-Barre syndrome, especially severe cases
Subacute autonomic failure after infection, surgery, or with suspected malignancy points to autoimmune/paraneoplastic ganglionopathy requiring workup
Acroparesthesias/burning feet and hands suggesting autonomic small-fiber neuropathy
Macroglossia suggesting amyloidosis; angiokeratoma suggesting Fabry disease
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on etiology. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension carries high mortality, approaching 44% over 30 months and exceeding 60% over 10 years in some series, and OH overall raises risk of falls, coronary disease, heart failure, stroke, and death. MSA progresses relentlessly to death typically 7-10 years after onset, though some survive beyond 10 years; early autonomic and bladder dysfunction, female sex, and rapid disability progression imply worse prognosis. Pure autonomic failure may evolve into a central synucleinopathy (PD, DLB, or MSA) after 5-10 years. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy increases diabetic mortality up to threefold. POTS is often chronic and self-perpetuating through deconditioning, but psychiatric comorbidity rates do not exceed the general population; graded exercise typically needs at least 6 months for benefit. Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy is important because it is treatable; about one-third of untreated seronegative cases improve spontaneously.
pitfalls: OH is frequently overlooked because most patients are asymptomatic or only mildly symptomatic, and chronic neurogenic OH may stay mild despite large BP drops due to cerebral autoregulation
Relying only on the absolute heart-rate rise can misclassify neurogenic OH; cardioactive drugs and intrinsic rhythm disturbances can blunt the expected tachycardia
Delayed OH may not appear until after 3-5 (sometimes 10) minutes of tilt, so short observation can miss it; postprandial and initial OH have distinct timing and triggers
Pharmacologic provocation during tilt testing increases sensitivity at the expense of specificity (normal subjects may faint)

Typical MSA MRI findings may appear only in advanced disease, so a normal early scan does not exclude it; the 'hot cross bun' sign is characteristic but not pathognomonic (also seen in some spinocerebellar atrophies)
Failing to screen for occult malignancy in autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy can miss a paraneoplastic small cell lung cancer, thymoma, or lymphoma
Overlap of preganglionic and postganglionic involvement occurs in autoimmune, paraneoplastic, and neurodegenerative disorders, so localization rules are not absolute
Attributing POTS symptoms to psychiatric disease; significant psychiatric disorder rates are no higher than in the general population
harrison.severityClassification: Orthostatic hypotension can be graded into four functional classes: class I, asymptomatic (may still have syncope/falls); class II, weekly-to-monthly symptoms with mild-to-moderate limitation of daily living; class III, more severe and frequent symptoms markedly limiting daily activities; class IV, daily severe symptoms causing significant disability. OH is further distinguished as nonneurogenic (compensatory HR rise >15 beats/min) versus neurogenic (HR rise <15 beats/min, or HR-rise/SBP-fall ratio <0.5 beats/min/mmHg), and by timing as initial, classical, delayed, and postprandial variants.
